channel.title: The Spiral and the Line
channel.description: A field notebook on the Riemann zeta function — six years of independent research, written up honestly, dead ends included.

item.title: Chapter 0: Prologue
item.description:
In April of 2025 I was deep in a conversation with an LLM, working through what looked like a real argument. The setup: a certain quantity decays like almost everywhere, but at two special points it decays much faster — instead. If is monotonic between those two points for large , a squeeze argument forces the entire interval between them down to that same fast decay rate. And since the generic behavior only matches that rate at an isolated point, the interval has no choice but to collapse — the two special points have to coincide.

It was a nice argument. It was also wrong in one specific place, and I caught it:

“I think your logic and reasoning mostly makes sense but I do notice one thing that is clearly wrong that you keep saying — you note that the generic decay rate of is not except when . This is demonstrably false because the generic decay rate when is . In fact… if we were to allow then we would have that the generic decay rate for is .”

The LLM had the mechanism right and one exponent wrong. Fixing it didn’t weaken the argument — it strengthened it, by closing off an edge case where the “generic” and “enhanced” decay rates could have coincided somewhere in the middle of the interval instead of only at an endpoint. We rebuilt the proof from there.

I’m telling you this story first because it’s the most honest way I know to describe what this project actually is: not “I asked an AI to solve the Riemann Hypothesis,” and not “I proved it myself and used a chatbot as a calculator,” but three years of a genuine back-and-forth — the most recent three of six I’ve now spent on this problem — where the LLM does things I can’t — hold enormous amounts of mathematical machinery in working memory, draft a rigorous-looking proof in seconds, try ten reformulations in an afternoon — and I do things it doesn’t reliably do on its own, chiefly: notice when a specific claim is wrong, insist on numerical verification, and refuse to let “this looks right” stand in for “this is proven.”

What the Riemann Hypothesis actually says

Take the Riemann zeta function, , extended (via analytic continuation) to all complex except . It has infinitely many “trivial” zeros at the negative even integers, and infinitely many more “nontrivial” zeros scattered through the strip . Every nontrivial zero ever computed — tens of billions of them — sits exactly on the line , the critical line. The Riemann Hypothesis is the conjecture that all of them do, always, with no exceptions. It’s been open since 1859. It’s one of the seven Clay Millennium Problems, and the only one from Hilbert’s original 1900 list that’s still unsolved. An enormous amount of modern number theory — the distribution of primes, chief among it — is built on results that assume RH is true, or that would sharpen dramatically if someone ever proved it.

Here’s what that actually looks like, computed directly rather than taken on faith. Pick a known zero and watch dive toward zero exactly at ; pick a height with nothing special about it and watch that dip simply not happen.

I am not going to prove it in this series. I want to say that on page one rather than let it hang in the air: the odds of an independent researcher resolving a problem this hard, that has resisted the best mathematicians alive for over 150 years, are close enough to zero that pretending otherwise would be dishonest. What I have instead is six years of genuinely trying — the last three of them documented closely enough to write this series from — across roughly six different angles, with a trail of what worked, what didn’t, and — a few times — something that stood on its own regardless of whether the big question ever closes.

Why this, specifically

I majored in Mathematics as an undergraduate in the mid-2000s, and it was a professor who first told me about the Millennium Problems — seven problems judged important enough, at the dawn of the 21st century, to carry a million-dollar bounty each. I was captivated and immediately out of my depth. I could barely parse most of the problem statements, let alone see a way in. If the hardest exam question I’d faced was a steep but climbable mountain, each Millennium Problem read like something from another planet — famous, immense, and not somewhere I had any business going. I filed them away as a piece of math history and moved on.

Years later, with a Ph.D. in Mathematics and some years working as a data scientist behind me, I was riding out the COVID-19 pandemic in a small studio apartment in New York City, with not much to do and a lot of time to do it in. That confinement turned out to be the catalyst: I went back and actually read all seven problem statements, and picked one. The one that pulled at me was the Riemann Hypothesis, because of its connection to prime numbers — the atoms of arithmetic, the thing that everything else in number theory is ultimately built from. I wanted, and still want, to find something simple in there. Not because I think the real answer will turn out to be simple — it almost certainly won’t — but because chasing simplicity is how I’ve always liked to work, and because it felt like a way to hand my younger self, the one who looked at those problem statements and saw only a wall, some kind of proof that the wall has footholds, even if I’m the one who never quite makes it over.

I’m writing this now from Tokyo, where I live these days — for what it’s worth, a city with its own centuries-old tradition of amateur mathematicians publicly working out geometry problems on wooden tablets (sangaku) and hanging them at shrines and temples, which feels like fitting company for a project like this one.

Six years in, I still don’t know how this ends. What follows is the record so far.

Why with an LLM

What I can describe precisely, because it’s all on the record: the shape of the collaboration changed as the tools did, but the division of labor has stayed remarkably consistent since the beginning. I bring the numerical intuition — decades of looking at these functions means I usually have a rough sense of where something interesting should be happening before I can say why. I insist on checking claims against real numbers: against the first 100,000 known nontrivial zeros, in one case. I catch the specific error, the way I did in April 2025, and a handful of other times across the notes this series draws from. The LLM brings breadth I don’t have — it can reach for a stationary-phase argument, a Poisson summation identity, or a result from a subfield I’ve never worked in, and draft it out fully formed in the time it takes me to describe the problem.

Neither of us gets there alone. That’s not a hedge — it’s the actual finding of three years of trying. The chapters that follow are the record of it: six reformulations of the same underlying obstruction, most of them dead ends, a couple of them real.

Next: Chapter 1 — The Moon — not where this started, but the first technique that left a real trail, three years into a project that actually began in 2020.

item.title: Chapter 1: The Moon
item.description:
A note on notation before we start: the earliest files in this project use for the offset from the critical line and for the height — the reverse of the convention I’ve used ever since and will use for the rest of this series. I’ve translated the original 2023 notes into the later convention below: is the height, is the offset, .

Three years of groundwork first

This wasn’t the first thing I tried. By late 2023 I’d already spent three years on this problem — most of it building up the machinery to even state a solution attempt cleanly, in a document I called, only half-jokingly, Primal Pilgrimage: number sets, basic geometry and trigonometry, Cauchy products, Cesàro summation, all rebuilt from scratch as scaffolding, ending in a “My Solution” section I could never quite finish writing. One early skeleton of that solution gets as far as “establish the doubling ratio… establish the order… conclude that is the only value that permits ” — three section headers in a row with nothing underneath them. I want that on the record too, because it’s true to how this actually went: long stretches of building tools before the first technique that actually produced a real inequality. The Moon, below, is that first technique.

The question

Take a partial sum of the alternating zeta series, , and look at its squared modulus, . Multiply the sum out against itself — every term against every other term — and you get a double sum, a Cauchy product, with one entry for every pair of indices. Group those entries by which term of the original series they came from, and you get something with a very specific structure: a grid, indexed by with , where each cell corresponds to the product .

The question I was chasing in late 2023 was simple to state and hard to answer: can this grid tell you, on its own — before you know anything about actual zeros — that is always at least as large as it would be with , i.e. right at the critical line? If that’s true for every , in the limit, you’ve got real leverage on where zeros can live.

Rays in a grid

Here’s the structural fact that makes the grid tractable. Every pair has a greatest common divisor — call it — and once you divide it out, and for some coprime pair . So instead of thinking of the grid as independent cells, think of it as a bundle of rays: one ray for every coprime pair , and along each ray, walks outward.

The reason this matters: the oscillatory phase attached to cell is — and that depends only on the direction of the ray, , not on how far out along it you are. Walk from to along a fixed ray and the phase doesn’t move at all. Only the magnitude changes, growing like .

A parity coincidence

The original series carries a sign, , and that sign has to land somewhere once everything gets folded into cosines and sines. It turns out to land on parity: whether is odd or even at a given point on a ray determines — cleanly, mechanically, via whether are themselves odd or even — whether that cell’s contribution comes in as a term or a term. Walk one more step along the ray, from to , and the label flips.

So a ray doesn’t alternate between two different phases — it alternates between two different labels on the same fixed phase, one step at a time: at , at , at , and so on.

The convexity payoff

This is where it turns into an actual argument rather than bookkeeping. Since , a consecutive pair of points on a ray — one labeled , the other — is literally a convex combination of two values of the function

evaluated at and . And is convex on for any real — three lines of calculus confirm . Jensen’s inequality then says the weighted combination you actually have is bounded below by evaluated at the weighted average of the two -values. Do this for both the -first and -first pairings on the same pair of points, average the two resulting bounds, and apply Jensen a second time: everything collapses to a clean lower bound of the form — exactly the value you’d get by setting from the start.

Try it

Drag the mixing weight and watch the amber dot (the weighted average you actually have) stay level with or above the teal dot (the curve at the weighted-average position) — for every weight, every curve shape.

Why “the moon”

I called this the moon scenario, because of the shape of what’s pairing up: two complementary crescents — the share of one point, the share of the next — that only complete each other, into a full convex combination, when you look at both halves together. Neither half alone is the whole picture; you need the linked pair.

Where it actually leads

Chained all the way through the grid, this gives a real, general fact: certain sums built from are bounded below by the value they’d take at , via nothing but Jensen’s inequality applied ray by ray. That’s a genuine result, not a numerical observation — and it was the first real technique of this project, eight months before the spiral picture in Chapter 2 gave the same underlying question a very different geometric face.

What it isn’t is a proof that the bound is ever strict — that the inequality can’t secretly be an equality at some . My own notes from that week end without answering that, mid-equation, on an unfinished attempt to compare against term by term. I’m leaving that exactly as honest as it actually was: a real piece of leverage, and an open door I didn’t walk through before moving on to the next idea.

Next: Chapter 2 — Finding the Spiral, December 2024.

item.title: Chapter 2: Finding the Spiral
item.description:
Previous: Chapter 1 — The Moon.

The picture

Fix a height on the critical strip and a real part . The partial sums

don’t converge as — but plotted in the complex plane, they don’t wander randomly either. They spiral: each new term rotates the running total by a bit more than the last (the phase of is , so consecutive terms rotate relative to each other by a shrinking angle), and the whole path winds in toward a fixed center. By December 2024 I had a name for this — the spiral picture — and enough of a feel for it to know it was worth pinning down exactly, not just admiring.

Pinning it down

Treat the real and imaginary parts of the partial sum as right-rule Riemann sum approximations to integrals, and likewise with . Integration by parts on both, then a little algebra with

collapses them to a closed form:

That’s exactly a spiral — traces a curve centered at the origin with radius , shrinking as grows for any and just barely failing to shrink at , which is the boundary where ’s defining series itself stops converging. The picture isn’t a metaphor; it’s a literal consequence of integrating an oscillating power function.

Where the real center is

is an approximation to the partial sum, not the partial sum itself, so define the difference and its limit . This — not the origin — is the actual center the true partial sums spiral around; only nails the shape and radius of the spiral, not quite where it’s centered. Getting a good, finite, computable estimate of turns out to matter a great deal later — it’s the seed of the pre-tail construction in Chapter 4 — but the qualitative picture is already the whole point of this chapter: , close to where the phase function’s stationary point sits, is a natural place to stop and read off where that center is, which is exactly why the truncation

that recurs throughout the rest of this project uses that specific cutoff.

The question that makes this more than a curiosity: where does the center sit? At a real, known zero of — one of the actual heights where — and exactly on the critical line, the center is the origin. Nudge away from , height held fixed, and the same spiral winds toward some other point entirely, not zero.

Try it

Pick a known zero from the list below, then drag the -offset fader off the critical line and watch the final point (the colored dot) leave the origin.

Each point along the path is a running total of ; the color goes from muted to full as runs from to the displayed cutoff. The path is drawn a few multiples past purely so the winding is legible to the eye — the small diamond marks where is actually evaluated. The fifteen preset heights are the first fifteen known nontrivial zeros of , so “locked” at isn’t a simulation — it’s the real function, doing the real thing.

Next: Chapter 3 — The Only Special Value, spring 2025.

item.title: Chapter 3: The Only Special Value
item.description:
I told the ending of one thread from this period already, in the Prologue: the argument that tried to force a zero-free interval around any hypothetical off-line zero by squeezing it between two points of “enhanced decay,” using monotonicity. That argument had a real gap even after I fixed the exponent error — the monotonicity it depended on was only ever “emergent for large ,” never actually proven, and when I pushed on that directly, the honest answer I got back amounted to restrict your attention to the range where it’s true and call the argument valid there. That’s not nothing, but it’s not a proof either.

A few days later I started over, with no preconceptions, on a differently-shaped version of the same question. This chapter is that attempt — and it’s the first time in this project that “why specifically” gets a clean, self-contained answer, even though, as you’ll see, it’s an answer to a narrower question than it sounds like at first.

Two ways for a partial sum to decay

Start with a rescaled partial sum built from the alternating series,

where plays the role of the offset from that this chapter cares about (translated to the rest of the series’ notation, ) and is the height. There’s a generic story and a special one.

Generically, converges to with error , so — every correction term is an integer power of . If happens to hold, the leading term vanishes and the next one, still an integer power, takes over: . Nothing about this story ever produces a half-integer power of . That mechanism, whatever it is, has to come from somewhere else.

Where the half-integer powers actually come from

Approximate the discrete alternating sum by a continuous oscillatory integral, . The exponent here is linear in — it has no interior stationary point on , only a contribution from the boundary at . The uniform asymptotic expansion of the incomplete gamma function that governs an integral like this naturally produces a ladder in powers of : — but only when the relevant parameter genuinely scales like , which a fixed, boundary-only phase doesn’t obviously give you. So the half-integer ladder is real, but it isn’t obviously available to this problem as stated.

The way to make it available — and this is the actual trick — is to temporarily deform the problem into one that has an honest interior saddle, then take the deformation away:

At this is exactly the original boundary-only integral. For any , the phase has a genuine, non-degenerate stationary point at , and the standard stationary-phase method applies cleanly, giving with corrections in the honest half-integer ladder

turns out to be an entire function of , and the stationary-phase expansion holds uniformly on compact sets in — which means the coefficients of that expansion, as functions of , extend holomorphically right down through , even though the saddle point itself has long since drifted out of by then. Set term by term in an expansion that was only derived for , and the half-integer ladder survives the trip. That’s the justification for treating as a real, available decay rate even in the purely boundary-driven original problem — not asserted, derived, from a problem that visibly has it.

The comparison that matters

So there are two independent asymptotic contributions in play: an endpoint term, decaying like , and a stationary-phase term, decaying like , smuggled in by the deformation argument above. Whichever one decays slower dominates, and a smaller term can only cancel against something of its own size — you can’t cancel an piece against an piece if one is genuinely larger, not without a coefficient that blows up with , which doesn’t happen here.

Try it

Drag and watch the two slopes on a log–log plot. They’re only ever parallel — the same order — at one place.

Only at do the two mechanisms land at exactly the same order, , and only then is mutual cancellation between them even arithmetically possible. Everywhere else, one term strictly dominates the other, and there’s nothing of the right size for it to cancel against.

What this does and doesn’t show

This is a real, self-contained argument, and it’s cleaner than anything in Chapter 1 — no monotonicity assumption doing quiet work in the background. But look closely at what it actually proves: it shows is the only point where these two particular mechanisms are the same order — a necessary condition for them to cancel, not a proof that they do. Nothing here rules out a completely different mechanism producing a zero somewhere else, and nothing here shows the coefficients in front of these two terms are ever actually equal and opposite at , only that they’re allowed to be.

It’s an honest, useful narrowing — the search space for “why the critical line” shrinks to one specific arithmetic coincidence of orders — but it’s not the whole argument. That gap between the only place cancellation is possible and cancellation actually happens is, in one disguise or another, exactly the gap this whole project keeps running into. It shows up again, worse, in Chapter 8 too.

One more thing worth flagging for later: the deformation trick here — adding a quadratic term to a phase to manufacture a saddle, then continuing back to the undeformed problem — isn’t a one-off. The same move resurfaces, independently rediscovered, in the pre-tail/tail machinery of Chapter 4 five months later, and again in 2026. I didn’t plan that continuity; it just kept being the right tool.

Next: Chapter 4 — Pre-tail and Tail, September–October 2025.

item.title: Chapter 4: Pre-tail and Tail
item.description:
By the fall of 2025, two pieces from earlier chapters were sitting next to each other without quite touching: the spiral picture from Chapter 2, where partial sums of wind toward a fixed center, and the endpoint-vs-saddle deformation trick from Chapter 3, which manufactures a genuine stationary point out of a boundary-only integral by adding a quadratic term to the phase and analytically continuing it away again. This chapter is where those two pieces actually fused — and where , the truncation length used everywhere from here on, stopped being a number I’d noticed worked well and became a number I could explain.

Why , precisely

Look at a single term of the alternating series at height : . Its phase, as a function of , is (the comes from folding the alternating sign into the exponential, the same move Chapter 1 made with cosines and sines). This phase has a genuine stationary point — no deformation required this time — exactly where , which is . There’s no trick here, no limit: this stationary point is really there, sitting inside the sum, for every height . If you’re going to split a partial sum into “the part before something interesting happens” and “the part after,” this is the honest place to make the cut.

The split

Define the finite pre-tail — a partial sum of , run out just past that stationary point, with a half-weighted final term for good measure:

(This is the same object that reappears, unchanged, as in Chapter 8 — I hadn’t settled on final notation yet in 2025, but the definition never moved again after this.) Partial sums of spiral toward a fixed center as more terms are added, and turns out to be a genuinely good approximation to that center — because is close to where consecutive terms’ magnitudes are comparable and their phases point in nearly opposite directions, which is exactly the point where a spiral’s trajectory is closest to having already settled.

The tail is everything after : , for the alternating series this time, and it’s where Chapter 3’s machinery earns its keep. Treated as a Fresnel-type integral around that same stationary point, the tail collapses to a closed form:

Notice what happens to the magnitude at specifically: the exponent vanishes, and for every height . The tail’s magnitude collapses to exactly — a single universal constant, independent of where on the critical line you are. Off the critical line, that magnitude drifts with ; on it, it doesn’t.

What this predicts at a zero

The eta and zeta functions are related by , and the same relation holds, approximately, between their pre-tail approximations. Combine that with the split above:

If is a genuine zero — so that both the true spiral center and its finite approximation vanish — this collapses to a clean prediction:

The pre-tail sum, at a real zero, should point in almost exactly the opposite direction from the tail’s closed form, with almost exactly the same magnitude, .

Try it

Pick a known zero and watch the two vectors, drawn tip to tail. Nudge off the critical line and watch the cancellation break.

Checking it against 100,000 real zeros

This is a concrete, falsifiable claim about actual known numbers, so I checked it against actual known numbers: the first 100,000 nontrivial zeros of , all of them verified to sit on the critical line. In every case, the pre-tail sum and the tail estimate come out pointing in nearly opposite directions, with modulus close to , exactly as predicted.

I want to be as precise about this as I was at the time: “I have no way of currently proving rigorously that this is always the case for all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function.” This is a strong, clean, checkable numerical regularity — a hundred thousand data points is not nothing — but it is numerics, not a proof, and I want to keep those two things visibly separate rather than let the size of the check do the work a derivation should.

Whatever happens to the rest of this project, I think this result stands on its own: a closed-form prediction about the geometry of truncated zeta and eta sums near real zeros, derived from first principles, checked at scale, and still — as far as I know — unexplained by anything deeper than “the numbers do this.”

Next: Chapter 5 — Rigidity and Its Discontents, December 2025.

item.title: Chapter 5: Rigidity and Its Discontents
item.description:
December 2025 opened with a smaller result first: a companion argument showing that a certain sign — an orientation, really, of one vector relative to another as you move along the critical line through a zero gap — obeys a clean first-order ODE, , whose solution can only change sign where itself passes through zero. Translated out of the differential-equations language: that orientation is locked in everywhere except at an actual zero of the function, or at one specific singular height where the machinery itself breaks down. It’s a real rigidity statement — nothing spontaneous is allowed to happen — but it’s about a sign, not a location, and it doesn’t by itself say anything about whether an off-line zero exists in the first place.

The bigger result that month reframes the whole project’s central question in the cleanest form it’s had yet, and I want to walk through it in full, because — unusually for this series — I don’t need to hedge the derivation itself. What I need to hedge is the one hypothesis it all rests on.

The symmetrized energy

Fix a height sitting strictly inside a gap between two consecutive zeros on the critical line, and let stand for (or its truncated approximation from earlier chapters) restricted to that height, varying only . Define — the function’s behavior as you step off the critical line by — and then symmetrize it:

This one substitution is what makes everything downstream exact rather than approximate. is even in by construction, no argument required — which means and every odd derivative vanishes at the origin automatically. Its Taylor expansion has no odd terms to worry about at all:

The transverse curvature

The quadratic coefficient works out exactly, with no approximation:

Divide by and call the result , the transverse curvature — literally how sharply the energy curves upward as you step away from the critical line at height . The quartic remainder is bounded, honestly and without cleverness, purely from how derivatives of grow: for in a suitably small range. Put the two together and divide through:

Nothing hidden, nothing vanishing mysteriously — every piece of this traces back to an explicit computation.

What it would take to get a zero-free strip

The right-hand side is positive — meaning can’t vanish there — exactly when . Choosing turns that into a single, clean condition on alone:

for some fixed constant and all sufficiently large in the gap. That’s the entire hypothesis. Not precise asymptotics, not a bound on every derivative, not RH itself assumed anywhere in the derivation — one lower bound, on one quantity, that’s directly computable from and its first two -derivatives at .

The Transverse Rigidity Theorem

Conditional. Fix a height strictly between two consecutive nontrivial zeros on the critical line, and suppose there exists such that the transverse curvature satisfies for all sufficiently large in that gap. Then there exists such that for all .

The width of the guaranteed zero-free strip, , isn’t an artifact of sloppy bookkeeping — it falls out naturally from balancing the quadratic term against the quartic remainder. The mechanism is entirely geometric (a curvature condition on an energy function), not arithmetic, and at no point does the argument assume anything about zeros existing or not existing off the line. It’s a real implication, cleanly stated, resting on exactly one unverified hypothesis.

Try it

Dial the curvature ratio below 1 and the guaranteed zero-free region vanishes entirely — not shrinks, vanishes. That threshold is the whole hypothesis.

What it does and doesn’t do

I want to be as direct as I was when I first wrote this down: this does not prove the Riemann Hypothesis. is exactly as open a question as RH itself, restated in different clothing — I haven’t shown it holds, only shown what would follow if it did, and that the numerics (after smoothing) look consistent with it. But converting one enormous, global, seemingly-intractable question into one precise, local, numerically-testable inequality — checkable gap by gap, height by height, against real computed values of — is not nothing. It’s the sharpest form the “why can’t zeros drift off the line” question takes anywhere in this project. Every version before this one bundled the mechanism and the missing piece together into something fuzzy; this version separates them cleanly, and hands you exactly one thing to go verify.

I haven’t verified it. Nobody has, as far as I know. But I know now precisely what I’d need.

Next: Chapter 6 — Only σ=1/2, Take Four, February 2026. Not yet posted — see the roadmap for what’s still coming.

item.title: Why the Critical-Line-Path Identity Isn’t a Coincidence

This is exactly the notebook’s closed form. The near-perfect numerical match isn’t a separate empirical discovery — it’s an exact algebraic consequence of three ingredients, only one of which (Step 3) isn’t already known to be exact.

Locating the remaining gap, and confirming it’s the right one

is not an exact identity for a finite truncation — it’s the classical “approximate functional equation” phenomenon (Euler–Maclaurin / Riemann–Siegel theory), true only up to a controllable error that shrinks as the truncation length grows relative to . So should approximate with an error that tracks the error in that functional equation — not an independent, unexplained residual.

I checked this directly: computed from and with no functional-equation assumption, compared it against the Step 3 prediction , and separately measured the actual relative error of . The two error curves track each other closely and both shrink as grows:

This is exactly the expected signature: the two error columns sit at the same order of magnitude at every and both fall as grows — confirming the diagnosis in Step 3 rather than leaving it as a plausible-sounding story.

What’s left, and why it’s a different kind of open problem

What remains is a single, classical-flavored estimate: a rigorous bound on

This is the same species of estimate that underlies the Riemann–Siegel formula and Euler–Maclaurin-based approximate functional equations for , which are rigorously established in the literature for various truncation schemes — though the specific scheme used throughout this project (, long compared to the classical “balanced” choice ) doesn’t appear to be a standard textbook case, so the bound would need deriving for this scheme specifically. That’s real work, but of a fundamentally different character than the gap in Chapter 6: it’s a quantitative asymptotic estimate about an explicit finite sum, not a claim that would resolve the Riemann Hypothesis if true. It’s worth doing carefully, both because it completes this identity rigorously and because the same estimate is very likely the missing ingredient in several other chapters’ hand-waved “the error term is small” steps.

Next step: derive the Euler–Maclaurin expansion of for directly — Poisson summation on the finite sum is the standard route — and extract an explicit power of for the error. That single derivation would upgrade this chapter’s headline result from “verified numerically, explained structurally” to “proved, with an explicit error bound.”
